clue.text: Implement of a dashing heart-stealer

parts.note: a suave charmer who steals hearts is a smooth operator, so his tool would be one that does his smooth-talking work; really a household tool for pressing clothes

explanation.surface: Asks what weapon a debonair ladykiller carries.
explanation.walkthrough: The heart-stealer suggests a smooth-talking charmer, a 'smoothie'; the implement is the old flat-iron heated on the stove to press laundry.
explanation.definitionFit: The cryptic picture of a charmer's tool leads to the heavy flat-iron once used to press linen.

clue.text: Prue's upset over a thé dansant; it's a bit much

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the first piece sits above the rest
upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters of Prue's are rearranged

parts.note: a tea dance, which, with tea as a bun, reads as a bun dance

explanation.surface: Prue is distressed by an afternoon tea dance; it is all too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges PRUES into SUPER, placed 'over' A and BUN DANCE: a thé dansant is a tea dance, and tea is turned into the bun eaten at it.
explanation.definitionFit: An excess or surplus is more than is needed, a bit too much.

clue.text: No Sir, say the birds!

indicators.note: say here asks the solver to give these words another reading, as a rearranged spelling

explanation.surface: Birds answer a gentleman with a refusal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' signals a new arrangement of NO SIR; the result is a scientific term for a region's birds.
explanation.definitionFit: The term means the avifauna, all the bird life of a region taken together.

clue.text: Celtic pose instrumental in stargazing

indicators.note: instrumental suggests something worked or played on, so the letters of Celtic pose are reworked

explanation.surface: A Celtic stance adopted while studying the stars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'instrumental' signals the rearrangement of CELTIC POSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to the astronomer's optical tube, the instrument of stargazing.

clue.text: Ordered aboard

definitions.meaning: arranged and in proper order, going smoothly

explanation.surface: A passenger is told to get on.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means set in motion in proper order, and also literally on a railway carriage.

clue.text: The lovely sisters familiar with fire-arms ?

definitions.meaning: Maria and Elizabeth, the celebrated Irish beauties of 18th-century London society

explanation.surface: Two beautiful sisters are handy with pistols.
explanation.walkthrough: The two sisters, who married the Earl of Coventry and the Duke of Hamilton, were the famous beauties of the 1750s.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the two celebrated beauties, and also the sport of hunting with guns.

clue.text: Who is here so — that would not be a Roman?" (J. Caesar)

definitions.text: Who is here so — that would not be a Roman?" (J. Caesar)

parts.words: Who is here so — that would not be a Roman?" (J. Caesar)
parts.note: Brutus's forum speech in Julius Caesar, Act 3 Scene 2; the blank is the adjective for an uncivilised, base person

explanation.surface: A gap-fill from Brutus's speech to the Roman crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: Brutus asks 'Who is here so base that would be a bondman? ... Who is here so rude that would not be a Roman?'
explanation.definitionFit: Brutus's word here means barbarous or uncivilised, lacking in culture.

clue.text: Stone Age mod ?

parts.note: a 'new stone' period, its name made of Greek elements for new and stone

explanation.surface: Asks what counted as modern among cavemen.
explanation.walkthrough: The name is Greek neo- (new, modern) and lithos (stone): the newer Stone Age.
explanation.definitionFit: The later Stone Age, the period of polished tools and early farming.

clue.text: Best men?

parts.note: not wedding attendants but people who insist everything be done flawlessly

explanation.surface: Asks about the bridegroom's attendants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best men' suggests weddings; read literally it is people who demand the very best.
explanation.definitionFit: People who will accept nothing short of flawless results.

clue.text: Daddy-Long-Legs in Oregon

definitions.meaning: the title of Jean Webster's 1912 novel, whose secret benefactor is Jervis, the guardian nicknamed after the spider
a city in the north-east of that American state, famous for its rodeo

explanation.surface: A gangly insect spotted in the American Northwest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daddy-Long-Legs' looks like the crane-fly; it is the novel, whose benefactor bears this surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The benefactor in Webster's novel has this surname, and a city in eastern Oregon shares it.

clue.text: Schwanda gives his bee impersonation

parts.note: Schwanda is the bagpiper hero of Weinberger's opera; a bagpipe's continuous bass pipes hum like a male bee

explanation.surface: An opera hero mimics a buzzing insect.
explanation.walkthrough: Schwanda the Bagpiper is a 1927 Czech opera; the bagpipe's sustained bass pipe shares its name with the male honeybee, so his playing is a bee impersonation.
explanation.definitionFit: The bass pipe of a bagpipe and the male honeybee share this name, both known for a low hum.

clue.text: " I remember, I remember, The —, red and white" (Hood)

definitions.text: " I remember, I remember, The —, red and white" (Hood)

parts.words: " I remember, I remember, The —, red and white" (Hood)
parts.note: a line from Thomas Hood's poem 'I Remember, I Remember'; the blank is the flowers he recalls from his childhood garden

explanation.surface: A gap-fill from Thomas Hood's nostalgic poem about his boyhood home.
explanation.walkthrough: The stanza continues 'The violets, and the lily-cups'; the blank is the red and white garden flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Hood's line names garden flowers of red and white, the blooms of the briar family.

clue.text: Discount for an American soldier with love

parts.note: an gives the letter A, the indefinite article
GI is the common term for a US enlisted soldier
love is nil in tennis, written as O

explanation.surface: Asks what price cut a GI romance earns.
explanation.definitionFit: In banking, the term is the premium or discount charged when exchanging one currency for another.

clue.text: Pet with any finish would be silky

definitions.meaning: a pet is a sulk or petty quarrel, a fit of pique

definitions.text: with any finish would be silky
definitions.meaning: with the letters of the word any added at the end, it becomes a sheer silky gauze fabric

explanation.surface: A domestic animal's coat, finished off, would feel smooth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' looks like an animal; it means a fit of temper. The second half adds ANY at the end to make TIFFANY, a fine silk gauze.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiff is a petty quarrel, the same thing as being in a pet or a sulk.

clue.text: Chaucer's gathering of 2

parts.note: Chaucer's poem of fowls, in which the birds meet to choose mates on St Valentine's Day

explanation.surface: A cross-reference to a medieval poet's assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: Chaucer's poem 'The Parlement of Foules' is an assembly of birds; 2 refers to the answer at 2-down.
explanation.definitionFit: An assembly or debate, as in Chaucer's poem about the birds' meeting.

clue.text: It caused a wedding-guest to beat his breast

definitions.text: It caused a wedding-guest to beat his breast

parts.words: It caused a wedding-guest to beat his breast
parts.note: from Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner, where the Wedding-Guest beats his breast on hearing a loud woodwind instrument from the feast

explanation.surface: A guest at a marriage feast is driven to anguish.
explanation.walkthrough: Coleridge writes: 'The Wedding-Guest here beat his breast, For he heard the loud' instrument, playing at the wedding he is missing while the Mariner holds him.
explanation.definitionFit: Coleridge names this deep woodwind instrument as the sound that made the Wedding-Guest beat his breast.

clue.text: A month for an old Irish clan over the hot coal

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means this piece sits above the next

parts.note: a sept is a clan or branch of a family in old Ireland
an ember is a glowing piece of coal

explanation.surface: A month when an Irish family gathers around the fire.
explanation.definitionFit: The ninth month of the year, first of autumn in the north.

clue.text: Art that proverbially outdoes the sword

definitions.text: Art that proverbially outdoes the sword

parts.words: Art that proverbially outdoes the sword
parts.note: the proverb says the pen is mightier than the sword, so the art is the one done with pen and pencil

explanation.surface: Names the art the proverb ranks above swordsmanship.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'the pen is mightier than the sword'; the art of the pen is drawing, engraving and lettering.
explanation.definitionFit: The art of drawing and engraving with pen or pencil is the visual art of the pen.

clue.text: The air of Elsinore

parts.note: in Hamlet, Act 1 Scene 4, on the battlements of Elsinore castle, Horatio calls the night air bitingly cold

explanation.surface: Describes the atmosphere at Hamlet's Danish castle.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet says 'The air bites shrewdly; it is very cold', and Horatio replies 'It is a nipping and an eager air.' 'Air' looks like a tune; it is the weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatio uses this adjective, meaning sharply biting cold, for the night air at Elsinore.

clue.text: Browning celebrated a toccata of his

definitions.text: Browning celebrated a toccata of his

parts.words: Browning celebrated a toccata of his
parts.note: Robert Browning's poem 'A Toccata of ...'s' is named after a Venetian composer

explanation.surface: Names the composer whose keyboard piece a Victorian poet praised.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's poem 'A Toccata of Galuppi's' addresses the 18th-century Venetian composer Baldassare.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venetian composer named in Browning's poem title about a toccata.

clue.text: As a prophet he was the end

definitions.text: As a prophet he was the end

parts.words: As a prophet he was the end
parts.note: the Old Testament closes with the book of the last of the minor prophets

explanation.surface: Calls a seer hopeless, in slang that he was the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He was the end' reads as slang for hopeless; literally his book is the last in the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: The minor prophet whose book is the final one in the Christian Old Testament.

clue.text: What was Sir Oliver doing text-wise?

definitions.text: What was Sir Oliver doing text-wise

parts.words: What was Sir Oliver doing text-wise
parts.note: Sir Oliver Martext is the hedge-priest in As You Like It, whose surname says he spoils the text

explanation.surface: Asks what a knight was doing with his reading.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's vicar in As You Like It is Sir Oliver Mar-text: his name says he damages scripture.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoiling or damaging, which is what the vicar's surname says he does to texts.

clue.text: One last word

parts.note: the word said at the close of a prayer or hymn, the final word spoken

explanation.surface: Someone asks to have the final say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One last word' sounds like a request to speak again; it is the word that ends a prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: This Hebrew word, meaning so be it, is said at the close of prayers and hymns.

clue.text: A violinist's uncomplimentary comment

definitions.meaning: a violinist's curved mark over notes meaning they are played smoothly in one bow

explanation.surface: A musician makes a snide remark.
explanation.definitionFit: In music the term is a curved line linking notes played legato; in speech it is an insulting aspersion.

clue.text: Gas escaping from a broken organ

indicators.note: a broken thing has its parts out of order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Air leaks from a damaged church instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges ORGAN into the noble gas; 'escaping from a' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: This inert noble gas makes up about one per cent of the atmosphere.

clue.text: Hudson Mansions

parts.note: W. H. Hudson's 1904 romance of the South American forest; the title's missing word is a colour

explanation.surface: Looks like the address of a block of flats.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a London apartment block; it is W. H. Hudson's novel with its first word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: The colour that opens the title of Hudson's forest romance, 'Green Mansions'.

clue.text: Chilly greeting

definitions.meaning: frozen rain pellets, an icy shower
a call of welcome or salute

explanation.surface: A cold welcome.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice pellets falling as precipitation, and a word of welcome or salute.

clue.text: He can run up a hood at a stretch

definitions.text: He can run up a hood at a stretch

parts.words: He can run up a hood at a stretch
parts.note: the hood is not sewn but the flared neck flap a certain snake spreads when it rears

explanation.surface: Praises a tailor who can make a hood quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run up a hood' suggests sewing in a hurry; the snake raises its hood by stretching its neck ribs.
explanation.definitionFit: This venomous snake spreads a hood of skin by stretching its neck ribs.

clue.text: Reduced to nothing in the sales ?

definitions.text: Reduced to nothing in the sales ?

parts.words: Reduced to nothing in the sales ?
parts.note: read literally, a thing with its price taken away entirely; really something too valuable to price

explanation.surface: Asks about goods so marked down they are free.
explanation.walkthrough: Read word by word it means 'without a price', as if sale reductions had reached zero; its real sense is beyond all price.
explanation.definitionFit: Something beyond valuation, too precious to be given a price at all.

clue.text: Sisyphean task is not one for the cryptogamist !

definitions.text: Sisyphean task is not one for the cryptogamist !

parts.words: Sisyphean task is not one for the cryptogamist !
parts.note: Sisyphus endlessly pushed a boulder uphill; a cryptogamist studies mosses and ferns, and the proverb says such moving boulders gather no moss

explanation.surface: Says a botanist would be wasted on Sisyphus's endless labour.
explanation.walkthrough: Sisyphus's punishment was rolling a boulder uphill for ever; the proverb 'a rolling stone gathers no moss' means a moss specialist (a cryptogamist) would find nothing on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Boulders being trundled along, which by the proverb gather no moss for a botanist to study.
